item.title: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation: Circulation and Reception
item.description: arXiv:2611.28384v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Louis Bachelier's Theorie de la speculation (1900) introduced a probabilistic model of Brownian motion in a study of financial fluctuations, five years before Einstein's physical theory. By connecting probability distributions with the heat equation and studying speculation and option valuation, Bachelier anticipated central developments in probability, physics, and mathematical finance. How widely did the thesis circulate before its broader significance was recognized? Drawing on library correspondence, surviving copies, accession registers, provenance marks, historical catalogues, and acquisition lists, this article reconstructs its international circulation and reception in two forms: the separate Gauthier-Villars dissertation and its publication in the Annales scientifiques de l'Ecole normale superieure. It identifies thirty-eight foreign academic institutions in the official dissertation exchange network for 1900 and documents its operation. University exchanges, commercial purchases, journal distribution, and personal presentations provided complementary channels. American holdings reveal its geographical reach, including receipt at Cornell in April 1900. Contemporary reviews and subsequent uses establish selective engagement in mathematics, actuarial science, and economics, including transmission without attribution. An examination of probability composition and diffusion clarifies the thesis's place in the history of stochastic processes and its relationship to physical Brownian motion. Columbia's journal volume, accessioned in 1901 and borrowed by Mandelbrot in 1961, connects early dissemination with renewed interest. Distinguishing availability from documented reading and use, the study shows that delayed recognition coexisted with early international circulation and a dispersed readership across scientific traditions.
item.dc:creator: Hector Giacomini

item.title: Newton's second law: not so elementary (as it may seem)
item.description: arXiv:1502.04303v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Introductory courses present Newton's second law either as a definition of force or as a law of nature, and in both cases leave unexplained why it holds only in a special class of reference frames. We give an operational reading of the law built on a single instrument, the spring balance. Its reading is a local fact on which all observers agree; in a given laboratory it defines the masses of bodies and a vector {\gamma} characterising the laboratory. Laboratories with $\gamma$ = 0 are, by definition, inertial. The empirical content of the second law is then the statement {\gamma} = -KA, where A is the acceleration of the laboratory measured kinematically from any inertial laboratory, and K is a universal constant that the choice of the newton as unit of force makes invisible. In this reading a spring balance is an accelerometer and an accelerometer is a dynamometer: both measure the specific force a-g familiar from inertial navigation. We discuss the hypotheses involved (universality of free fall, absence of rotation, locality) and the relation with Newton's own formulation.
item.dc:creator: Ledo Stefanini, Giancarlo Reali

item.title: Newton's Second Law: A Structural Necessity of Mechanics Constrained by Excluded Perpetual Motion and Universal Free Fall
item.description: arXiv:2608.06266v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For over three centuries, Newton's second law (F = ma) has governed mechanics with extraordinary success, while its epistemic warrant has remained empirical. That merely empirical contingency vanishes once mechanics is constrained by two principles: the principle of excluded perpetual motion (PEPM) with its pre-Newtonian phenomenological content and the weak equivalence principle (WEP) with universal free fall as its primitive content. The PEPM secures the applicability of Suppes' measurement-theoretic framework to gravitational mass and force, exposing the formal structure latent in their empirical manifestations and establishing both as independent primitives. Gravity bridges statics and kinematics in Stevin's and Galileo's inclined-plane arguments, where the common sine factor in force and acceleration cancels in F/a. Cycle arguments under the PEPM extend this result to arbitrary force mechanisms, establishing F/a as object-intrinsic and securing inertial mass as a well-defined physical quantity. Further constrained by universal free fall, the resulting quantitative structure compels the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass, with Newton's second law as the operational expression of that equivalence. Direct implications include constraints on modified-inertia MOND that follow from the PEPM alone. The PEPM also places free-fall and torsion-balance experiments on equal footing as tests of the WEP. Together with the WEP, the derivation further grounds both the dimensional reduction of mechanics and the location-invariance of the Kibble-balance realization of the SI kilogram. Deeper still, Newton's second law derives its necessity from exclusion and invariance principles whose scope extends beyond mechanics itself.
